content_html:
Before Ramadan, many Muslims look for a Quran khatam Ramadan schedule (a plan to complete the whole Quran) that fits their day, so they do not start strong and stop in the middle ten nights. Here you will find the exact pages per day, three ready-made plans (30, 15 and 10 days), a printable table, a split across the five prayers, a time estimate, and a catch-up plan.

Ramadan 1448 AH is expected to begin around 8 February 2027 according to the Umm al-Qura calendar, and the actual start depends on sighting the crescent moon. If you are reading this in Rajab or Sha'ban, now is the best time to choose and practise your plan.

How many pages a day to finish the Quran in Ramadan?

To complete the Quran once in Ramadan, read one juz (part) a day, which is about 20 pages of the Madinah Mushaf (604 pages). The easiest split is 4 pages after each of the five daily prayers. If the month is 29 days, read about 21 pages a day. For a khatam in 15 days read two juz a day (about 40 pages), and in 10 days three juz a day (about 60 pages).

These numbers are based on the Madinah Mushaf printed by the King Fahd Complex, the edition most used in mosques and apps:

  • 604 pages from the start of Al-Fatihah to the end of Surah An-Nas.
  • 30 juz, each about 20 pages (the first juz is 21 pages, and the last is a little longer because of the many headings of its short surahs).
  • 60 hizb, two in each juz, each about 10 pages.
  • 240 quarters (rub'), four in each hizb, each about two and a half pages.

The exact maths: 604 ÷ 30 ≈ 20.1 pages a day, and 604 ÷ 29 ≈ 20.8 pages a day. So the daily juz is the simplest unit: the Mushaf is already divided by it, and you need not count pages.

Why do we aim to complete the Quran in Ramadan?

Ramadan is the month of the Quran; its revelation began in it. Allah says:

﴿شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ الَّذِي أُنزِلَ فِيهِ الْقُرْآنُ هُدًى لِّلنَّاسِ وَبَيِّنَاتٍ مِّنَ الْهُدَىٰ وَالْفُرْقَانِ﴾

"The month of Ramadan [is that] in which was revealed the Qur'an, a guidance for the people and clear proofs of guidance and criterion." (Surah Al-Baqarah 2:185, translation: Sahih International)

The Prophet ﷺ used to study the Quran with Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, on the nights of Ramadan. Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said:

"The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was the most generous of people, and he was most generous in Ramadan when Jibril met him. Jibril used to meet him every night of Ramadan and study the Quran with him." (Sahih al-Bukhari 6)

In the final year of his life ﷺ, Jibril reviewed the Quran with him twice. Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "He used to review the Quran with the Prophet ﷺ once every year, and he reviewed it with him twice in the year he passed away." (Sahih al-Bukhari 4998). The Prophet ﷺ told his daughter Fatimah about this in confidence, and said he saw it as a sign that his time had come (Sahih al-Bukhari 3624 and Sahih Muslim 2450).

From this, scholars took that reciting and studying the Quran a great deal in Ramadan is recommended. No text makes completing it in the month obligatory, but a khatam is a beautiful goal that gathers the heart on the Book of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever reads a letter from the Book of Allah will have a good deed for it, and a good deed is rewarded tenfold." (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2910, and at-Tirmidhi said: hasan sahih)

As for the narration "O Allah, bless us in Rajab and Sha'ban and let us reach Ramadan", which spreads widely at this time of year, hadith scholars have graded it weak. A Muslim may ask Allah to let them reach Ramadan in any words, without attributing this wording to the Prophet ﷺ.

How do I complete the Quran in Ramadan in 30 days? (printable daily table)

The basic plan that suits most people is one juz every day. Next to each day is where that juz begins in the Madinah Mushaf (surah and verse), in case your Mushaf does not mark it. Print the table and tick the last column each day:

If the month is 29 days: do not wait to find out. Add about two-thirds of a page a day (21 pages instead of 20), or read one and a quarter juz each of the last ten nights. You will finish on the twenty-ninth night, and if the month has thirty days you have a spare day for review.

Why start your plan two days before the month?

Many people fall behind in the first days as sleep and meal times change. Reading two juz at the end of Sha'ban builds a reserve. It is not a requirement, just a practical aid.

Splitting your Ramadan khatam across the five prayers

The surest way to keep going is to tie your portion to the prayers, which are fixed appointments. Instead of hunting for a free hour, read a few pages after each prayer:

PlanDaily portionAfter FajrAfter DhuhrAfter AsrAfter MaghribAfter Isha
Khatam in 30 days1 juz (20 pages)4 pages4 pages4 pages4 pages4 pages
Khatam in 15 days (two in the month)2 juz (40 pages)8 pages8 pages8 pages8 pages8 pages
Khatam in 10 days (three in the month)3 juz (60 pages)12 pages12 pages12 pages12 pages12 pages

A note on the maths: 4 pages × 5 prayers × 30 days = 600 pages, leaving only 4 pages. You can cover them by reading one extra page on four days of the month, or by following the juz boundaries instead of counting pages. Uneven pages between prayers are fine; just finish the day's portion before you sleep.

You can also split by hizb and quarter: one hizb after Fajr and the other across the remaining prayers. A juz has eight quarters, so two after Fajr and one and a half after each other prayer completes it.

How long does it take to finish the Quran?

Speed varies with your tajweed (rules of recitation) and pace. On average a page takes 2 to 3 minutes of moderate, measured recitation. This approximate table helps you choose:

PlanPages per dayDaily time (approx.)Time after each prayer (approx.)
One khatam a month, in or outside Ramadan20 pages40–60 minutes8–12 minutes
Khatam in 29 days21 pages42–63 minutes8–13 minutes
Khatam in 15 days40 pages80–120 minutes16–24 minutes
Khatam in 10 days60 pages120–180 minutes24–36 minutes

Time yourself reading a whole juz before Ramadan, then choose the plan you can manage on your busiest days, not your freest. If you are slower because you are learning tajweed or reflecting, you are doing great good, and the thirty-day plan is enough.

A khatam in 15 or 10 days: who is it for?

The 15-day plan: two juz a day

For those who have already done a one-juz-a-day khatam and want more, or who are on holiday in Ramadan. Two juz a day (about 40 pages) finishes once mid-month and again at the end. Read one juz by day and one at night so no sitting is too heavy.

The 10-day plan: three juz a day

This needs two hours or more a day, so it suits those used to reciting a lot. Some use it for the last ten nights only: one juz a day for twenty days, then three juz a night for a full khatam, seeking Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Decree).

And outside Ramadan?

A monthly khatam is the same one-juz plan, the one the Prophet ﷺ first advised Abdullah ibn Amr (may Allah be pleased with them both), as below. Keep it after Ramadan, or halve it and finish every two months.

Is it better to do many khatams or to reflect?

Abdullah ibn Amr (may Allah be pleased with them both) reported that the Prophet ﷺ said to him:

"Recite the Quran in a month." I said: "I have the strength to do more," until he said: "Then recite it in seven days, and do not do it in less than that." (Sahih al-Bukhari 5054; Sahih Muslim 1159 reports it with similar wording)

In a narration in Abu Dawud (1394) and at-Tirmidhi (2949), also from Abdullah ibn Amr, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever recites it in less than three days does not understand it." At-Tirmidhi said it is hasan sahih, and al-Albani graded it sahih in Sahih Abi Dawud, as shown in the hadith encyclopedia of Dorar al-Saniyyah (in Arabic).

The early generations varied: some completed the Quran every seven days, some every three, and some are reported to have read more in Ramadan for the virtue of the time. Many scholars took the prohibition of less than three days to describe what is usual, or someone who does not understand what they read, agreeing that the greatest aim is understanding and acting on it.

Allah says:

﴿كِتَابٌ أَنزَلْنَاهُ إِلَيْكَ مُبَارَكٌ لِّيَدَّبَّرُوا آيَاتِهِ وَلِيَتَذَكَّرَ أُولُو الْأَلْبَابِ﴾

"[This is] a blessed Book which We have revealed to you, [O Muhammad], that they might reflect upon its verses and that those of understanding would be reminded." (Surah Sad 38:29, translation: Sahih International)

So do not make the number of khatams a goal in itself. One khatam recited with care and understanding is better than many rushed ones that leave nothing in the heart. A balanced approach: a recitation khatam with the daily table, plus a page or two a day with tafsir for reflection. If you are not sure which tafsir to choose, read our comparison of Tafsir as-Sa'di and Tafsir al-Muyassar.

How do I make up a missed portion of my Ramadan khatam?

Everyone falls behind sometimes: travel, illness, work or short nights. Just do not let it make you abandon the plan. It is established in Sahih Muslim (747) that whoever sleeps and misses his nightly portion (hizb), or part of it, and reads it between the Fajr and Dhuhr prayers, it is recorded for him as if he had read it at night. This is a basis for making up regular portions. Here is a practical catch-up plan:

  1. Work out what is left: subtract the juz read from 30 and divide by the days remaining. Example: after day ten you have read 7 juz, so 23 remain over 20 days, about one and a quarter juz a day (around 23 pages).
  2. Spread the catch-up, do not pile it up: do not read it all in one day and burn out; add two or three pages after each prayer until you catch up.
  3. Use your day off: make your weekly day off a catch-up day and read one extra juz.
  4. Accept an adjusted plan: if you missed a lot, finish a few days after Eid. A late khatam is better than an abandoned one.

How do I organise a family khatam in Ramadan?

A family khatam gathers the household around the Quran. The two common ways are:

  • Dividing the thirty juz among family members: five people each take six juz over the month, about one juz every five days, completing one khatam together. With six people, each takes five.
  • A family khatam every few days: with many readers (ten, say) each taking three juz, the family completes a khatam every few days, depending on their pace.

Each person is rewarded for what they themselves read. The group khatam is for encouragement and cooperation; it does not replace a personal khatam for anyone who wants one. Put the juz table on the fridge or in the family chat, tick each juz when done, and gather on completion day for a simple family du'a.

What are suitable Ramadan Quran goals for children?

A child is not asked to do what an adult does; the aim is love of the Quran, not exhaustion. Suggested goals by age:

  • Ages 4 to 6: listening to a short surah every day, and memorising one short surah each week.
  • Ages 7 to 9: reading one page a day with a parent, or completing Juz Amma (the 30th juz) during the month.
  • Ages 10 and over: half a juz a day, or completing the last three juz of the Mushaf, or taking part in the family khatam with one or two juz.

Reward them with praise or a star on their own chart, and keep reading time short and fixed, such as right after iftar. For daily adhkar suited to young children, see our guide to daily adhkar for kids.

How do I read the Quran in Ramadan alongside Taraweeh and work?

Ramadan days are full of fasting, work, iftar and Taraweeh, so smart timing matters more than long sessions:

  • After Fajr: the calmest time, with a clear mind after suhoor; give it the largest share.
  • Before Maghrib: time often lost waiting; good for the remaining pages and du'a before iftar.
  • In Taraweeh: many imams complete the Quran over the month, about a juz a night. Listening attentively is great worship, but it does not count towards your personal khatam if you want to read it yourself, so do both.
  • After Taraweeh: read the juz the imam will recite the next night, so you understand it better when you hear it in prayer.
  • On the move: listen to a reciter you love, which keeps your heart connected even when you cannot read.

Rafiq Al-Taa, our free, ad-free app with an Arabic interface, has the complete 604-page Madinah Mushaf. Tap any verse for its tafsir, listen to many reciters, and download surahs to hear offline. Its Ta'ati ("My Worship") section has a daily Quran box with a streak counter. It has no khatam planner, so print this article's tables to use alongside it. The app is coming soon to Google Play; more on offline listening in our guide to the Quran offline app.

How can women in menstruation or postnatal bleeding stay connected to the Quran in Ramadan?

Days of hayd (menstruation) or nifas (postnatal bleeding) can interrupt a woman's plan. In summary:

  • Touching the Mushaf: most scholars hold that a menstruating woman should not touch the Mushaf directly. Many of them hold that she may read with a barrier such as a glove, or from a phone, since many contemporary scholars do not give a device the ruling of the Mushaf.
  • Reciting from memory: there is a well-known difference of opinion. Most jurists of the Hanafi, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools hold that a menstruating woman should not recite the Quran, while the Malikis, and a number of careful scholars who favoured their view, permit it, especially when needed, such as fear of forgetting, or teaching and learning.
  • What is not disputed: she may listen to the Quran, read books of tafsir, and engage in dhikr (remembrance), tasbih (saying SubhanAllah), istighfar (seeking forgiveness) and du'a, which are wide doors of reward.

So use those days to listen to the juz in your table or read its tafsir, then resume once pure and make up what you missed as above. This is a summary of the well-known views, so consult the scholars in your country about your own situation.

Summary: choose your plan before the month begins

A Quran khatam Ramadan schedule is simple maths: one juz a day is about 20 pages, or 4 pages after each prayer, and you finish in thirty days. If you want more, two juz a day gives a khatam every 15 days, and three juz a khatam every 10 days. More important than the count is reading with reflection, catching up without despair, and leaving Ramadan with a steady daily portion. To link your portion to the rest of your daily worship, use our daily worship tracker. To check hadiths further, see the Dorar hadith encyclopedia, and to read the verse with its tafsirs, see Surah Al-Baqarah 2:185 on quran.com.

faq.q: How many pages should I read a day to finish the Quran in Ramadan?
faq.a: The Madinah Mushaf has 604 pages, so you need about 20 pages a day to finish in thirty days, which is one juz a day. The easiest split is 4 pages after each of the five daily prayers. If the month is twenty-nine days, read about 21 pages a day, or add a little in the last ten nights.

faq.q: How much should I read a day to finish the Quran twice in Ramadan?
faq.a: For two khatams in the month, read two juz a day, about 40 pages, which is 8 pages after each prayer, finishing once every fifteen days. This takes roughly one hour twenty minutes to two hours a day depending on your speed, so choose this plan only if your time allows it without rushing your recitation.

faq.q: Is it allowed to complete the Quran in less than three days?
faq.a: The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said: whoever recites it in less than three days does not understand it, narrated by Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi and graded sahih by al-Albani. The early generations differed in how often they completed it, and many scholars understood the hadith to mean that someone who rushes this much usually does not understand. The greatest aim is understanding and reflection, not the number of khatams.

faq.q: What should I do if I fall behind my Ramadan khatam schedule?
faq.a: Work out the juz remaining and divide them by the days left, then spread the extra over the prayers by adding two or three pages after each prayer, instead of reading everything you missed in one day. Use your day off to catch up, and if you still cannot, finish the khatam after Ramadan. A late khatam is better than giving up.

faq.q: Does the imam's recitation in Taraweeh count towards my khatam?
faq.a: Listening attentively to the imam in Taraweeh is a great act of worship and you are rewarded for it, but if your plan is to read the Quran yourself, keep your personal portion separate. A useful idea is to read, after Taraweeh, the juz the imam will recite the next night, so you gain both the reward and the understanding.
